newsitem.title: UK: Pound's leap postpones UK growth pickup -economist.
newsitem.headline: Pound's leap postpones UK growth pickup -economist.

text.p: The pound's strength is postponing Britain's economic revival and eating into corporate profits, leading British economist Patrick Minford said on Sunday.
And those hoping that the British currency will ease back soon are misguided, he added.

"If the pound continues at its present level throughout 1997, we are in for a return to the recession growth rates, two percent or so, we had for most of the past two years," Minford said in a report from his Liverpool Research Group at Liverpool University.

He said increasing uncertainty about the success of European economic and monetary union (EMU), scheduled to start in January 1999, leaves the pound looking like a safe haven and unlikely to fall back despite its 17 percent trade-weighted rally since August last year.

Against the German mark, which Minford said is overvalued regardless of EMU, sterling has shot up from about 2.27 marks last summer to as high as 2.77 last week, only a whisker below the level it was before it crashed out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism in September 1992.
Furthermore, official UK interest rates at six percent, are three percentage points above the German discount rate -- a differential that should see pounds bought for marks.

"A rising pound is like an invisible poison. It spreads quietly through the trading corporate's limbs, destroying gross profit margins roughly one percent off for every one percent on the pound," Minford said.
"Investment plans in manufacturing are no doubt further being put off."

Official figures out last week showed manufacturing output was just 1.6 percent higher than a year ago in January, while annual consumer spending growth chugs along at about four percent -- a clearly unbalanced economy.
The only way to stop sterling in its tracks, and get the economy back on an even keel is to "break the market's psychology by a sharp reverse in monetary policy for a significant time," Minford said.
"There is no shame in taking detours around threatening obstacles when you are on a long journey," he said. "The high pound is now such a threat. Let us defuse it."
